content.:tutorial/content:
If we want to add (or subtract) three or more matrices, all operations should be done elementwise. For example, suppose

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then we can calculate ${A}+{B}-{C}$ by performing the operations on each corresponding entry, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B-C & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+(-1)-0 \\ 1+2-5 \\ -1+0-(-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Performing the operations on each corresponding entry, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(B-C) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}-(\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 & -5 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1-0 & -1-(-5) \\ 2-1 & 0-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1-(-1) & 0-4 \\ 2-1 & -2-(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Sum or Difference of Three or More Matrices

content.:tutorial/content:
Since addition and subtraction of matrices are performed elementwise, they have the same properties as addition and subtraction of real numbers.

For example, if $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are three $m \times n$ matrices then we can add them in any order:

$$
(A+B)+C = A+(B+C) = A+B+C
$$

Moreover, we can distribute a subtraction over matrices in parentheses:

$$
A - (B + C) = A - B - C
$$
content.:tutorial/title: Properties of Matrix Addition and Subtraction

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we simplify the expression by distributing the subtraction over the matrices in the parentheses: 

$$
\begin{aligned}A+C-(B+A) & =A+C-B-A \\  & =\cancel{A}+C-B-\cancel{A} \\  & =C-B\end{aligned}
$$

We are left with a single subtraction. So, we subtract the corresponding entries of the two matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}C-B & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -6 & 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3-3 & -1-(-1) \\ 1-2 & 2-0 \\ -6-(-4) & 1-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Sum or Difference of Three or More Matrices Using Distributivity

content.:tutorial/content:
We add two matrices by adding the corresponding entries. We can only do this if they have the same number of rows and columns, that is, they have the same dimensions.

For example, consider the matrices

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

We see that both $A$ and $B$ are $2\times 2$ matrices, so we can add them. The sum ${A} + {B}\,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+1 & 3+0 \\ 2+0 & 4+(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, the sum of two matrices is another matrix with the same dimensions.

We can subtract matrices in the same way that we add matrices: we subtract the corresponding entries. Again, we can only do this if they have the same number of rows and columns, that is, they have the same dimensions.

For example, consider the matrices

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

We see that both $A$ and $B$ are $2\times 2$ matrices, so, we can subtract them. The difference ${A} - {B}\,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A-B & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-1 & 3-0 \\ 2-0 & 4-(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, the difference of two matrices is another matrix with the same dimensions.

To simplify an expression like $-(3+b)$, we need to **distribute** the negative sign across each of the terms inside the parentheses. This can be accomplished by treating the negative sign like multiplication by $(-1)$. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
- (3 + b) &=  \\
(-1)(3 + b) &=  \\
(-1) \cdot 3 + (-1) \cdot b &=  \\
- 3 + (-b) &=  \\
&= - 3 - b
\end{aligned}
$$

In these cases, the negative sign in front of the parentheses represents the $-1$. However, to save space, only the negative sign is shown.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the negative sign as multiplication by $(-1)\mathbin$:

$$
\begin{aligned} - \left(3n+\dfrac{1}{2}k \right) \\ &= (-1) \left(3n+\dfrac{1}{2}k \right) \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we distribute the $(-1)$ to each term in the parentheses, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned} (-1) \left(3n+\dfrac{1}{2}k \right) \\ &= (-1) (3n)+(-1) \left(\dfrac{1}{2}k \right) \\ &= -3n+ \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}k \right) \\ &= -3n-\dfrac{1}{2}k \end{aligned}
$$

content.:knowledge-point/title: Distributing the Negative Sign over the Sum of Two Terms

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the negative sign as multiplication by $(-1)\mathbin$:

$$
\begin{aligned} -(2x-1.3) \\ &= (-1)(2x-1.3) \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we distribute the $(-1)$ to each term in the parentheses, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned} (-1)(2x-1.3) \\ &= (-1) (2x)-(-1) (1.3) \\ &= -2x-(-1.3) \\ &= -2x+1.3 \end{aligned}
$$

content.:knowledge-point/title: Distributing the Negative Sign over the Difference of Two Terms

content.:tutorial/content:
By distributing the negative sign across each of the terms inside the parentheses, we're merely changing the sign of each term. In other words:

- If a term was *positive* inside the parentheses, it becomes *negative*.
- If a term was *negative* inside the parentheses, it becomes *positive*.

content.:knowledge-point/title: Distributing the Negative over More Than Two Terms
